column4: The source section's root سمو derives the name from height; the command puts اسم beside الأعلى and asks the hearer to glorify it, making that raised-name image explicit.
The source section treats a name as a raised sign; here the name of the Lord of majesty and honor is itself declared blessed, giving that name public praise.
The source section links the name to being raised; this verse joins houses God permits to be raised with His name being mentioned in them, turning elevation into a setting for invocation.
The source section's dictionary account of سمو links a name with raised mention; God says He raised the Messenger's ذكر, directly describing an honored name carried into remembrance.
The source section's dictionary form سَمِيّ means a peer who could bear the same name; after commanding worship and patience, this verse asks whether anyone is His namesake, marking His uniqueness.
The source section presents names as signs used in calling; this verse explicitly lets the caller say Allah or al-Rahman and says the beautiful names belong to Him.
The source section connects a name with recognition and invocation; this verse says Allah owns the beautiful names and commands people to call Him by them.
The source section's image of the name as a sign finds a direct formulation in this verse: Allah alone has the beautiful names.
The source section treats a name as a sign that makes its bearer known; after naming Allah as Creator, this verse says the beautiful names belong to Him.
The source section says a name is the identifying sign under which an act begins; the first command to read is explicitly بِاسْمِ رَبِّكَ, placing reading under the Creator's name.
The source section describes a written name identifying who speaks; Solomon's letter identifies its sender and begins بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم, so the name both authenticates and frames the message.
The source section's letter scene calls the message a noble book; this verse supplies that letter's reception, while 27:30 identifies Solomon as sender and gives its opening name.
The source section describes Nuh putting the name over the ark's movement and anchorage; the verse tells its passengers that its sailing and stopping are بسم الله.
The source section joins names to knowledge and recognition; God teaches Adam all the names, making naming a divinely taught means of knowing created things.
The source section says names identify what is known; after God teaches Adam the names in 2:31, Adam states them here before the angels, showing that knowledge at work.
The source section's dictionary root وسم includes توسّم, reading a trace; this verse calls the ruins signs for الْمُتَوَسِّمِينَ, people who discern marks.
The source section's root وسم means a branding mark; this verse uses سَنَسِمُهُ for a mark placed on a man's snout, making the identifying brand a public disgrace.
The source section's dictionary root وسم concerns a mark by which someone is recognized; this verse says the needy are تعرفهم بسيماهم, though their restraint hides their need from casual notice.
The source section's image joins a raised sign to recognition; people on الأعراف recognize others by their marks, combining height and visible identification in one scene.
The source section links raised signs with recognition; the men on الأعراف call those they know by their marks, continuing the scene of 7:46 and making their identification active.
The source section's trace-reading sense of وسم is explicit here: the Prophet will know hypocrites by their marks and by لحن القول, a visible and verbal trace.
The source section describes a mark by which a person is known; this verse says the believers' سيما is on their faces from prostration, a bodily sign of their worship.
The source section's dictionary root وسم describes identifying marks; this verse says wrongdoers are known by their marks before being seized by forelocks and feet.
The source section's root علم includes signs that distinguish and guide; this verse names عَلَامَاتٍ and the stars as waymarks by which travelers find direction.
The source section's dictionary form عَلَم includes a raised standard or landmark; this verse calls ships like الأعلام among God's signs, making a visible height a marker in the sea.
The source section says creation itself makes the Lord knowable; God promises to show His signs in the horizons and in people themselves until the truth becomes clear.
The source section expands its sign-image to all creation; this verse locates signs in the earth for those certain of faith.
The source section treats created kinds as signs; this verse directs attention to the human self as another sign to be read.
The source section says the whole created world is marked by signs; this verse states directly that signs fill the heavens and earth for believers.
The source section makes living creation a set of signs; this verse points to human creation and the creatures God disperses as signs for the certain.
The source section presents creation as a field of readable signs; this verse names night and day, rain reviving earth, and winds as signs for people who reason.
The source section extends the sign-image across creation; this verse lists heavens, earth, ships, rain, creatures, winds, and clouds as signs for people who reason.
The source section presents created things as signs of their Lord; this verse makes the creation of heavens and earth and the alternation of night and day signs for people of understanding.
The source section links a sign with what can be known from it; this verse describes the sun, moon, and their measured phases as signs by which people know years and reckoning.
The source section reads the created order as signs; this verse identifies the alternation of night and day and all creation as signs for those mindful of God.
The source section joins height and signs; here God raises the heavens and subjects the sun and moon, then details signs for people certain of meeting Him.
The source section defines a sign as a trace that distinguishes one thing from another; this verse says adjacent fields watered by one water yield different produce, a difference God calls signs.
The source section says each created kind can serve as a sign; this verse points to crops, olives, palms, grapes, and fruits as signs for people who reflect.
The source section reads the world as the Lord's signs; this verse names night, day, sun, moon, and stars as signs for people who reason.
The source section's root علم concerns a distinguishing trace; this verse points to earth's varied colors as a sign for people who remember.
The source section says created kinds are signs that distinguish; this verse names differences of languages and colors among people as signs for those who know.
The source section treats variety in creation as readable signs; this verse points to differing fruit and colored mountain bands as evidence for observers.
The source section says each created kind bears a distinguishing sign; this verse extends differing colors to people, beasts, and livestock, and links knowledge to reverence.
The source section makes the created world signs of Allah; this verse calls night, day, sun, and moon His signs but forbids worshipping those signs instead of their Creator.
The source section calls each created kind a sign; this verse explicitly names the spread of living creatures through the heavens and earth among God's signs.
The source section says creation is an identifying sign; this verse points to the spread earth, its mountains, and every beautiful pair brought forth from it.
The source section says signs let the Lord be recognized; this verse calls the created scene of 50:7 a reminder and insight for every servant who turns back.
The source section says each created kind is itself a sign; this verse says God made pairs of everything so people may remember.
The source section places Allah's name over Nuh's ark; this verse says Nuh and the ship's companions were saved and the ship made an آية for all worlds.
The source section presents Nuh's ark moving under Allah's name; this verse says the surviving ark was left as a sign and asks who will take warning.
The source section's dictionary note defines توسّم as seeing a trace; this verse asks people to look at آثار رحمة الله in the revived earth, a visible trace of mercy.
The source section's trace-reading sense of وسم has a close counterpart in this verse: God records what people sent ahead and their آثار, preserving deeds and their traces.
The source section says signs can be read from what remains; this verse has the shaken earth report its أخبار, making the ground disclose its trace.
The source section's image treats traces as evidence; this verse says the earth's disclosure in 99:4 happens because its Lord inspired it.
The source section describes signs that identify their bearers; here people emerge in separate groups to be shown their deeds, the setting for the visible accounting in 99:7–8.
The source section's dictionary account of توسّم includes recognizing good traces; this verse says even an atom's weight of good will be seen.
The source section's dictionary account of توسّم includes recognizing evil traces; this verse completes 99:7 by making even an atom's weight of evil visible.
The source section says an علم is a sign by which something is known; this verse says Allah will show His signs and people will recognize them.
The source section's trace-reading image distinguishes seeing from blindness; this verse calls the Lord's proofs insight and says whoever sees benefits himself while the blind harms himself.
The source section describes a mark that makes someone recognizable; this verse attaches each person's record to their neck and brings it out as a readable book.
The source section defines a name as what lets a thing be recognized; this verse says the People of the Book recognize the Messenger as they recognize their sons, though some conceal the truth.
The source section treats a sign as a means of knowing its bearer; this verse says the People of the Book recognize him as they recognize their sons, then says the losers do not believe.
The source section describes a written name as an identifying trace; this verse says the unlettered Messenger is found written in the Torah and Gospel.
The source section says a name identifies the thing itself; this verse commands that adopted sons be called by their fathers' names, making accurate naming an act of justice.
The source section defines the name as a sign identifying its bearer; Jesus announces a messenger after him by the specific identifying name أَحْمَدُ.
The source section's dictionary form سَمِيّ means a namesake; Zachariah's son is named Yahya, and God says He had made no namesake for him before.
The source section links names with raised mention; this verse says الْكَلِمُ الطَّيِّبُ ascends to God and righteous deeds raise it, joining good speech with elevation.
The source section says a good name spreads among people; this verse says Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob were given a lofty truthful mention among later generations.
The source section's image treats public mention as a name that endures; Abraham asks God to give him a truthful mention among later generations.
The source section describes a good name traveling among people; after rescuing Nuh, God says He left him in the remembrance of later generations.
The source section's good-name image is completed here: the later generations' remembrance of Nuh takes the form of the greeting, “Peace upon Nuh.”
The source section describes names that remain in public memory; after Ibrahim's trial, God says He left him in later generations' remembrance.
The source section says a good name circulates as praise; the next verse makes Ibrahim's preserved mention a greeting of peace.
The source section treats lasting mention as a name's public trace; God says He left Musa and Harun in the remembrance of later generations.
The source section's good-name image is completed by this greeting to Musa and Harun, the honored form of their lasting mention.
The source section says a name can remain among people; God says He left Ilyas in the remembrance of later generations.
The source section's lasting-name image is completed here by the greeting of peace upon Ilyas.
The source section presents a good name as a sign raised among people; this verse pictures a good word as a tree with a firm root and branches reaching heaven.
The source section describes a good name circulating among people; the good tree of 14:24 bears fruit continually by its Lord's leave.
The source section says created kinds and places can be signs; this verse explicitly calls Safa and Marwa among Allah's شعائر and gives them a role in pilgrimage.
The source section's dictionary form عَلَم is a sign or landmark; this verse names clear signs in the sanctuary, including Ibrahim's station.
The source section reads the world as signs that direct recognition; this verse says honoring Allah's شعائر comes from the hearts' piety.
The source section says each created kind can be a sign and that the name marks an act; this verse calls sacrificial camels Allah's شعائر and commands His name over them.
The source section links Allah's name with the created worlds; this verse says each community is given a rite so it can mention His name over the livestock He provided.
The source section places a name over an act; this verse tells pilgrims to mention Allah's name over the livestock He provided.
The source section treats a sign as a designation that must be recognized; this verse protects Allah's شعائر, offerings, and garlanded animals from violation.
The source section describes a mark that distinguishes an object; this verse names the Sacred House, offerings, and garlands as divinely appointed signs and supports for people.
The source section says a name identifies what an act is placed under; this verse permits eating from the animal over which Allah's name has been mentioned.
The source section's name-as-designation image meets this verse's question why people would not eat what bears Allah's mentioned name, after God's prohibitions have been explained.
The source section says a name marks an act's allegiance; this verse forbids eating what lacks Allah's name and calls that omission فسق, making the name a boundary.
The source section's root علم includes knowing; this verse uses it for trained hunting animals, then commands Allah's name over their catch, joining learned recognition to invocation.
The source section says a name is a sign made known through mention; this verse describes worship houses where Allah's name is much mentioned.
The source section treats Allah's name as a public sign; this verse condemns those who prevent His name from being mentioned in mosques.
The source section gives the name an identifying and devotional role; this command says to remember the Lord's name and devote oneself to Him.
The source section connects the Lord's name with worship; this command calls for remembering it morning and evening.
The source section joins name and worship; this verse says the successful person remembers the Lord's name and prays.
The source section pairs the Lord's name with elevation and praise; this verse commands glorification in the name of the Lord, the Great.
The source section treats the divine name as a sign honored in speech; this verse ends by commanding glorification in the name of the Lord, the Great.
The source section describes a name as what the caller invokes; this verse makes that act a direct divine command, promising response to those who call upon Him.
The source section names invocation of Allah; this verse draws the boundary that mosques belong to Allah and no one else is to be invoked alongside Him.
The source section shows a name used in calling; this verse contrasts hearts recoiling when Allah alone is mentioned with their joy when other beings are mentioned.
The source section says a name should identify a real bearer; Hud challenges his people over names they and their fathers invented without authority from Allah.
The source section warns that a raised name can lack the thing it should identify; Yusuf says the gods people worship are only names they and their fathers assigned without authority.
The source section says names mark what is truly known; this verse calls the idols people name only names, with no authority sent by God.
The source section presents الرحمن as a name by which Allah is called; this verse stages people rejecting that very name with “What is al-Rahman?”
The source section says Nuh's ark has a named movement and anchorage; after the voyage, this verse asks God for a blessed landing, echoing the ark's stopping-place.
The source section links the name's height with knowing; this verse says God raises believers and those given knowledge by degrees, giving elevation to knowledge itself.
The source section says each created kind is an identifying sign; this verse calls animals on earth and birds communities like people, then gathers all to their Lord.
The source section describes every created kind as a sign in itself; this verse distinguishes creatures by their ways of moving—belly, two legs, or four.
The source section says the created order is a sign of its maker; this verse says God created the heavens and earth in truth and that this is a sign for believers.
The source section treats each living kind as a sign; this verse points to birds above with wings spread and folded and asks who holds them except the Merciful.
The source section says created kinds make their Lord knowable; this verse directs attention to birds held in the sky and calls their flight signs for believers.
The source section's trace-reading image includes signs of good and evil; after the mercy trace in 30:50, this verse shows wind-yellowed crops as the reverse sign.
The source section places Allah's name over Nuh's voyage; this verse has those aboard say praise to Allah for rescue, supplying the worshipful response during that same passage.
The source section links names with knowledge; the reading command of 96:1 continues here with the Lord teaching by the pen.
The source section says names make things knowable; this verse completes 96:4 by saying God taught humanity what it did not know.
The source section's good-name image meets the firm-word theme of 14:24–26; here God makes believers firm by a firm word in this life and the next.
The source section describes reading a person's visible trace; this verse says the bliss of Paradise can be recognized in the brightness of faces.
The source section's dictionary root وسم describes recognizing a camel by a cut ear or brand; this verse condemns Satan's command to slit cattle ears as a false religious designation.
The source section describes animal marks used to classify a camel; this verse rejects the invented statuses of bahira, sa'iba, wasila, and hami as labels Allah did not assign.
The source section's brand is a trace by which an animal is known; here hoarded gold and silver are heated to burn foreheads, sides, and backs, turning a mark into punishment.

The source section's dictionary root وسم concerns an identifying brand; this verse calls worldly horses الْمُسَوَّمَةِ, apparently marked horses, though this is a different Arabic root and the sense is uncertain.
The source section describes marks burned on animals; this verse calls Lut's stones مُسَوَّمَة, marked for the wrongdoers, a distinct Qur'anic marked-object image rather than the source root وسم.
The source section's mark makes an object identifiable; this verse repeats the marked stones for the transgressors, explicitly locating their designation with God.
The source section's trace-readers are directed to Lut's overturned city in 15:75; this verse supplies the visible ruin that their marks reveal.
The source section's trace-reading scene continues after 15:75; this verse locates the ruined city on a lasting road, leaving the sign exposed to passersby.
The source section calls the trace readable by perceptive people; this verse completes the city passage by naming it a sign for believers.

The source section says Allah's name marks a designation; this verse describes people assigning livestock categories and omitting Allah's name over some animals, which it calls fabrication against Him.
The source section says naming makes knowledge possible; after Adam's names in 2:31, the angels say their knowledge is only what God taught them, locating its source.
The source section's Adam passage makes names the means by which creation becomes knowable; this preceding verse sets the question of Adam's role that the naming lesson answers.
The source section's good-name image meets its reversal in this verse: a bad word is like a rotten tree uprooted from the earth with no stability.
The source section describes a mark that lets its bearer be known; this verse says some recognized what came to them and then rejected it, making recognition itself a moral boundary.
The source section defines the name as a sign of the named being; the angel identifies Mary's promised child by the name al-Masih, Isa son of Maryam.
The source section says created things are signs that point beyond themselves; Ibrahim first calls the setting star his lord, then rejects it when it sets, separating a sign from its Creator.
The source section treats the created world as signs of Allah; Ibrahim repeats the test with the setting moon, showing that a visible heavenly marker is not itself the Lord.
The source section's raised-sign image meets its boundary here: Ibrahim calls the sun greater, yet rejects it when it sets and turns toward its Creator.
The source section says creation is a sign pointing to its Lord; after the star, moon, and sun set, Ibrahim turns his face to the Creator of the heavens and earth.
The source section's root علم includes distinguishing signs; this verse says stars are waymarks for travel through land and sea and signs for people who know.
The source section reads creation as signs; this verse names lightning, rain, and earth revived after death as signs for people who understand.
The source section's trace-reading image meets rain that visibly revives the earth; this verse calls that revival a sign for people who listen.
The source section says each living kind is a sign; this verse introduces the bee's divinely guided homes and work, which 16:69 develops as a sign.
The source section treats each species as a sign; this verse describes the bee's varied drink and honey and says in that is a sign for people who reflect.
The source section says created kinds make the Lord knowable; this verse directs people to the earth's many noble plant pairs, the scene called a sign in 26:8.
The source section expands its sign-image to creation; this verse explicitly calls the plant variety of 26:7 a sign, though most people do not believe.
The source section treats created kinds as signs; this verse supplies the concrete creation—sky, mountains, and dispersed animals—that 31:11 contrasts with what false gods made.
The source section contrasts true signs with names lacking a bearer; this verse calls the visible order Allah's creation and challenges people to show what rivals created.
The source section says creation's kinds are signs; this verse names paired fruits, rivers, mountains, and night and day as signs for people who reflect.
The source section's dictionary form الأعلام evokes raised sea-markers; after ships like landmarks in 42:32, this verse says their stillness on the sea is a sign for the patient and grateful.
The source section asks readers to discern traces; this verse points to earth revived after death and says God has made His signs clear for people who reason.
The source section links the divine name with invocation; this verse describes believers whose hearts respond when Allah is mentioned and whose faith grows when His verses are recited.
The source section gives the Lord's name an audible devotional role; this verse says skins shiver and hearts soften when Allah is mentioned during recitation.
The source section presents الرحمن as a name used in calling; Mary invokes that name for refuge when the stranger appears before her.
The source section identifies Allah as the greatest name and connects naming with worship; God says “I am Allah,” declares no deity but Him, and commands worship and remembrance.
The source section says every created kind is a sign; this verse says all in the heavens and earth, including birds, glorify Allah, and each knows its prayer and praise.
The source section says created things are signs of their Lord, not the Lord Himself; this verse lists sun, moon, stars, mountains, trees, and animals prostrating to Allah.
The source section describes a visible trace that identifies its bearer; this verse shows one group marked by bright, joyful faces on the Day of Judgment.
The source section's mark can distinguish good from evil; this verse gives the opposing sign, faces on that Day covered with dust.
The source section's trace-reading image includes contrary marks; this verse completes the dusty faces of 80:40 with darkness covering them.
